overview: An environment variable is a named value (a key=value pair like DATABASE_URL=postgres://...) that lives in a running process's environment; programs read these values to configure themselves without hardcoding anything in the code.

When a process starts a child process, the child inherits a copy of the parent's environment variables - this is why 'export' matters: it marks a variable to be passed down to child programs (like your Python ETL script), while a plain shell variable stays local to the shell.

PATH is one special environment variable: a colon-separated list of directories the shell searches to find executables, so when you type 'python' the shell walks PATH in order and runs the first matching program it finds.
learningObjectives: Explain what an environment variable is, view and set them (printenv, env, echo $VAR, export, unset), and understand how child processes inherit them.
Describe how PATH works as an ordered, colon-separated search list, resolve a command with 'which'/'command -v', and safely add a directory to PATH.
Persist variables across sessions in ~/.bashrc / ~/.zshrc / ~/.profile, and use environment variables and .env files to configure data pipelines and store secrets without hardcoding them.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: An environment variable is a dynamic, named value stored in the environment of a running process and made available to that process and, when exported, to its child processes. In a Unix-like shell, a variable defined as NAME=value is a shell-local variable visible only to the current shell; the 'export' builtin adds it to the environment block that the kernel copies (via fork/exec) into every child process the shell launches. The environment is thus per-process and inherited downward, never upward or sideways. PATH is a standardized environment variable containing a colon-separated list of directories; when you invoke a command by name, the shell searches these directories left to right and executes the first matching executable, so ordering determines precedence. Persistence is achieved by writing export statements into shell startup files (~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc, ~/.profile) or system-wide files (/etc/environment, /etc/profile.d/), which the shell reads when it starts, re-creating the variables for each new session.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Think of an environment variable as a sticky note attached to a running program that says something like 'DATABASE_URL = this address'. The program can peek at the note whenever it needs that information, instead of having it written permanently into its code. When a program launches another program (a child), it hands the child a photocopy of all its sticky notes - but only the notes you marked with 'export'. Notes you did not export stay in your pocket (the shell) and never get copied. PATH is a very important sticky note: it is a list of folders, separated by colons, telling the shell where to look for programs. When you type 'python', the shell reads down that list of folders in order and runs the first 'python' it bumps into. Because the notes vanish when the program ends, you write them into a startup file (like ~/.bashrc) so a fresh copy is stuck on every new terminal you open.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Environment variables originate in Unix in the 1970s at Bell Labs, where the concept of a per-process environment passed through the exec system call let programs be configured without recompiling them; PATH appeared early as a way to let users run programs by name without typing full directory paths. The Bourne shell (1979) and later the C shell, Korn shell, and Bash (1989) all built on the same environment-inheritance model, and Zsh (1990, and the default on modern macOS since 2019) followed suit. The rise of cloud computing and containers made environment variables central to configuration: the influential 'Twelve-Factor App' methodology (2011, from Heroku) codified 'store config in the environment' as a best practice for keeping code identical across dev, staging, and production. The .env file convention and libraries like python-dotenv, plus dedicated secrets managers (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault), grew up around the same idea - keep credentials and settings out of source code and inject them through the environment.

whyItMatters.business: Storing configuration and credentials in environment variables instead of code lets the same application run unchanged in development, staging, and production, so teams ship faster and avoid the costly, embarrassing incidents that come from committing a database password or API key into a public repository.
whyItMatters.engineering: Environment variables are how a data engineer wires a pipeline to its database, warehouse, and cloud services without editing code; getting PATH right is what makes the correct Python, dbt, or spark-submit run, and misunderstanding either is a leading cause of 'works on my machine' failures.
whyItMatters.scalability: Injecting config through the environment lets one build artifact (a Docker image, a package) be deployed to hundreds of machines and many environments, each parameterized differently, without rebuilding - the foundation of reproducible, fleet-wide deployment.
whyItMatters.cost: Externalizing settings prevents accidentally shipping expensive misconfigurations (pointing a dev job at a production warehouse) and avoids the enormous cost of leaked cloud credentials, which attackers can use to spin up resources and run up huge bills.
whyItMatters.reliability: When configuration lives in the environment, promoting code from staging to production changes nothing in the code path, dramatically reducing the risk of environment-specific bugs; and a correct PATH guarantees jobs invoke the exact interpreter and tools they were tested against.

coreComponents.name: Environment variables and export
coreComponents.definition: Named key=value pairs held in a process's environment; a plain assignment (NAME=value) is shell-local, while 'export NAME=value' marks it to be inherited by child processes.
coreComponents.purpose: To pass configuration and secrets to programs at run time without hardcoding them, and to control which values flow down to the child processes a shell launches.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Store settings (like DATABASE_URL or LOG_LEVEL), be readable by any program via its language's environment API (os.environ in Python), and, when exported, be copied into every child process the shell starts.
coreComponents.examples: export DATABASE_URL=postgres://... | export AWS_REGION=us-east-1 | LOCAL_ONLY=temp (shell-local, not exported) | export LOG_LEVEL=INFO

coreComponents.name: PATH (executable search list)
coreComponents.definition: A special environment variable holding a colon-separated list of directories the shell searches, left to right, to find the program matching a command you type.
coreComponents.purpose: To let you run programs by name (python, git, dbt) without typing their full filesystem path, and to control which version runs when several exist.
coreComponents.responsibilities: List the directories of executables, be searched in order so the first match wins, and be extended (usually by prepending '$HOME/bin' or a virtualenv's bin) to make new tools discoverable.
coreComponents.examples: echo $PATH | export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH" | export PATH="$PATH:/opt/spark/bin" | which python3

coreComponents.name: Inspection tools (printenv, env, echo, which, command -v)
coreComponents.definition: Commands that show the current environment or resolve where a command comes from: printenv/env list exported variables, echo $VAR prints one, and which/command -v report which executable a name resolves to via PATH.
coreComponents.purpose: To see what configuration a process actually has and to debug PATH problems by revealing exactly which program will run.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Print all exported variables (env, printenv), print a single variable (echo "$VAR" or printenv VAR), and resolve a command name to its full path using the current PATH (which, command -v, type).
coreComponents.examples: printenv | env | echo "$DATABASE_URL" | printenv PATH | which python3 | command -v dbt

coreComponents.name: Persistence files (~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc, ~/.profile, /etc/environment)
coreComponents.definition: Startup files the shell reads when it launches; putting 'export' lines in them re-creates your variables and PATH additions for every new session, while /etc/environment sets system-wide variables for all users.
coreComponents.purpose: To make environment variables and PATH changes survive beyond the current terminal, so you do not have to re-type them every time you open a shell.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Hold export statements executed at shell start (~/.bashrc for interactive Bash, ~/.zshrc for Zsh, ~/.profile for login shells), define machine-wide variables (/etc/environment), and be re-read on demand with 'source'.

internalWorking: Every process the kernel runs is given an environment block - a list of NAME=value strings - alongside its arguments. A program reads this block through its language's API (getenv in C, os.environ in Python, process.env in Node), and the shell exposes it to you as variables you reference with a leading '$' (like $HOME).

When you write NAME=value in the shell, you create a shell-local variable stored only in the shell's own memory. The 'export' builtin flips a flag marking that variable for export, which moves it into the environment block that will be handed to children; this is the entire difference between a variable that a child program can see and one it cannot.

Starting a program triggers fork() (the shell makes a copy of itself) followed by exec() (the copy replaces itself with the target program), and during exec the kernel copies the parent's environment block into the new process. Because it is a copy, changes a child makes to its environment never propagate back up to the parent - environment flow is strictly downward.

For PATH resolution, when you type a bare command name the shell splits $PATH on colons and, for each directory left to right, checks whether an executable file of that name exists there; it runs the first one it finds and stops searching. This is why order matters: a directory earlier in PATH shadows a program of the same name later in PATH. (Shells also cache these lookups with 'hash' for speed.)

Persistence works because a new shell, at startup, executes your startup file line by line. An 'export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"' line re-reads the current PATH and prepends your directory, rebuilding the desired environment from scratch for that session; the variables themselves never persisted - the instructions to re-create them did. This is why editing ~/.bashrc has no effect on already-open shells until you 'source' it.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Shell startup reads ~/.bashrc / ~/.zshrc / ~/.profile -> export statements build the environment (including PATH) -> you set/inspect vars (export, printenv, echo $VAR) -> you run a command by name -> shell searches PATH left to right for the executable -> shell forks + execs the program -> kernel copies the exported environment into the child -> program reads config via os.environ -> child exits, its environment discarded
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. You open a new terminal. The shell starts and reads ~/.zshrc, running each 'export' line - this rebuilds PATH (for example, prepending your virtualenv and $HOME/bin) and sets standing variables like AWS_REGION and LOG_LEVEL for this session.

2. You need to point an ETL job at the database, so you run 'export DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@db.internal:5432/analytics'. The variable is now in your shell's environment and marked for export, so any program you launch next will inherit it.

3. You verify with 'printenv DATABASE_URL' (or 'echo "$DATABASE_URL"') to confirm the value is set correctly, and 'which python3' to confirm which interpreter will run when you type python3 - the shell resolves it against PATH.

4. You run 'python3 etl.py'. The shell forks and execs Python, and the kernel copies the exported environment - including DATABASE_URL and AWS_REGION - into the new Python process. Inside etl.py, 'os.environ["DATABASE_URL"]' returns the value, so the code connects without any credentials written in the source.

5. The Python process finishes and its environment is discarded. Your DATABASE_URL still exists in the shell (the parent) because children cannot alter the parent's environment; when you close the terminal, though, the shell-set value is gone - only what is written into ~/.zshrc (or a .env file the script loads) comes back next time.

keyTerminology.meaning: A named value (NAME=value) stored in a process's environment and readable by that process; if exported, it is also inherited by child processes.
keyTerminology.importance: It is the standard, code-free way to configure programs and pass secrets, so it underlies almost all pipeline and application configuration.

keyTerminology.meaning: The shell builtin that marks a variable to be included in the environment handed to child processes; without it a variable is shell-local and invisible to programs you launch.
keyTerminology.importance: It is the single distinction between a value your Python script can read (exported) and one it cannot, so forgetting export is a classic 'why is my variable empty?' bug.

keyTerminology.meaning: A colon-separated list of directories the shell searches, in order, to locate the executable for a command name.
keyTerminology.importance: It decides which program actually runs when you type a name; a wrong or wrongly ordered PATH is why the 'wrong python' or a 'command not found' happens.

keyTerminology.meaning: A script the shell runs when it starts; putting export lines there re-creates your variables and PATH for every new session.
keyTerminology.importance: It is how environment changes become permanent; understanding which file runs (login vs interactive, Bash vs Zsh) is essential to make settings stick.

keyTerminology.meaning: A local file of KEY=value lines that a library (like python-dotenv) loads into the environment at program start, so you keep config out of code without exporting each variable by hand.
keyTerminology.importance: It is the everyday pattern for local development and secret handling in data projects, and knowing to gitignore it prevents leaking credentials.

importantConcepts.concept: Shell-local vs exported: why your variable is 'empty' in Python
importantConcepts.explanation: A plain assignment like 'DATABASE_URL=postgres://...' creates a variable that lives only inside your current shell. You can echo it and use it in the shell, but the moment you launch another program (python, a subshell, a script), that program's environment does not contain it - because it was never marked for export, the kernel did not copy it into the child. The fix is 'export DATABASE_URL=postgres://...', which adds it to the environment block that fork/exec hands down to children. This is the number-one confusion for beginners: 'I set the variable but my script says it's None'. Remember the rule - programs you run inherit only exported variables, and inheritance is one-way (parent to child), so setting a variable inside a script never changes the shell that launched it.

importantConcepts.concept: PATH ordering and precedence: first match wins
importantConcepts.explanation: PATH is not a set, it is an ordered list, and the shell runs the first matching executable it finds as it scans directories left to right. This means where you insert a directory changes behavior. Prepending ('export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"') makes your directory take priority, so your version of a tool shadows any system version of the same name; appending ('export PATH="$PATH:/opt/tools/bin"') makes it a fallback used only if nothing earlier matches. This is exactly how a Python virtual environment works: activating it prepends the venv's bin directory to PATH so that 'python' and 'pip' resolve to the venv's copies instead of the system ones. When 'which python3' surprises you, echo $PATH and read it left to right - the answer is almost always ordering.

importantConcepts.concept: Never hardcode secrets; inject them through the environment
importantConcepts.explanation: Credentials such as AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, and DATABASE_URL must never be written into source code or committed to Git, because repositories get shared, forked, and leaked, and a leaked key can cost real money and expose real data. The standard practice is to keep them out of code and provide them through environment variables at run time: your script reads os.environ, and the values are supplied by the shell, a .env file loaded locally (and gitignored), a CI/CD secret store, or a dedicated secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault) in production. This also enables the same code to use different credentials per environment. The related discipline is the Twelve-Factor 'config in the environment' principle: anything that varies between deploys (endpoints, credentials, feature flags) belongs in the environment, not the codebase.

importantConcepts.concept: Persistence and which startup file runs
importantConcepts.explanation: Environment variables you set in a terminal disappear when that terminal closes, because the environment is per-process. To make them permanent you write 'export' lines into a startup file that the shell reads on launch - but which file matters. Interactive Bash sessions read ~/.bashrc; login shells read ~/.profile or ~/.bash_profile; Zsh (the macOS default) reads ~/.zshrc. System-wide values for all users go in /etc/environment or a file under /etc/profile.d/. A subtle trap: editing a startup file does not affect shells that are already open, because they read it only at startup - you must open a new terminal or run 'source ~/.bashrc' to re-execute it. Choosing the wrong file (putting a variable in ~/.bashrc when your job runs via a non-interactive login shell, for example) is a common reason a variable 'works in my terminal but not in cron'.

variationsAndTypes: **Scope of variables:** shell-local (NAME=value, current shell only), exported (export NAME=value, inherited by children), and per-command (VAR=value command, set only for that single invocation).

**Where variables are defined:** interactively in the shell, in per-user startup files (~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc, ~/.profile), in system-wide files (/etc/environment, /etc/profile.d/), or by orchestrators (Docker -e, Kubernetes env, systemd, CI/CD secret stores).

**Common data-engineering variables:** connection/config like DATABASE_URL and AWS_REGION, credentials like AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID / AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, behavior flags like LOG_LEVEL and ENV=production, and language settings like PYTHONPATH and VIRTUAL_ENV.
**PATH-style list variables:** PATH (executables), PYTHONPATH (Python import search), LD_LIBRARY_PATH (shared libraries), and MANPATH - all colon-separated ordered lists searched left to right.

**Ways to load config safely:** direct export, a .env file loaded with python-dotenv or 'set -a; source .env; set +a', secret injection from CI/CD, and secrets managers (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault) for production.
advantages: **Decouples config from code:** the same script or image runs unchanged across dev, staging, and production, with behavior controlled entirely by the environment.
**Keeps secrets out of source control:** credentials are injected at run time rather than committed, reducing the risk and blast radius of leaks.
**Universally supported:** every language and OS can read environment variables (os.environ, getenv, process.env), so the pattern is portable across tools and platforms.
**Easy to override per run:** you can set a variable for a single command (VAR=value cmd) or per session, making one-off tests and overrides trivial.
**PATH makes tooling seamless:** you invoke programs by name and control exactly which version runs, which is what makes virtualenvs and per-project toolchains work.
disadvantages: **Invisible and easy to get wrong:** a missing 'export', a typo in a name, or a wrong PATH order fails silently or with a confusing error, and the state is not visible in the code.

**Not inherently secret:** environment variables can be read by anyone who can inspect the process (and may appear in logs or crash dumps), so they are convenient but not a strong secrets vault by themselves.
**Session-bound by default:** values vanish when the shell closes unless persisted, and persistence depends on getting the right startup file, which is easy to confuse.
**Global namespace collisions:** a variable set by one tool can clash with or be overwritten by another (or leak into an unrelated child), causing surprising behavior.
**Stringly-typed and unvalidated:** everything is a string with no schema, so a malformed URL or a numeric flag stored as text is not caught until the program tries to use it.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use environment variables for anything that varies between deployments or must stay out of code: connection strings, credentials, region/endpoint settings, and behavior flags. Use a .env file (gitignored) for local development convenience, and prepend to PATH to make a project-specific toolchain (like a virtualenv) take precedence. Use them to keep one build artifact deployable to many environments.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid environment variables as your only secrets store for sensitive production credentials - use a real secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault) and inject at run time. Avoid stuffing large or structured config (many settings, nested data) into the environment; use a config file for that. Avoid committing .env files, and avoid editing PATH blindly (prepending untrusted directories can let a malicious 'python' shadow the real one).

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Think of a company where each employee (process) gets a welcome packet when they start their first day. The packet contains labeled instructions like 'The database is at this address' and 'Log at this level' - these are the environment variables. When an employee hires an assistant (starts a child process), they photocopy their packet and hand it over - but only the pages they chose to share (the exported ones); private notes stay in their own drawer. The company directory that tells you which floor to go to for 'Accounting' or 'IT', read from the top down until you find the first match, is PATH - and if two departments are both labeled 'IT', you walk into whichever one is listed first. The standard welcome packet that every new hire automatically receives - printed fresh each morning - is your ~/.bashrc: it re-creates the instructions for every new session, because the packets themselves are thrown away when the employee leaves for the day.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Setting a variable in one terminal makes it available everywhere.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Environment variables are per-process. A variable you set in one terminal exists only in that shell (and the children it launches). Another terminal, another user, or a cron job will not see it. To make it available broadly you must persist it in a startup file that every relevant shell reads, or provide it explicitly to the program that needs it.

export only marks a variable to be inherited by child processes of the current shell; it does nothing for future sessions. When you close the terminal the value is gone. To persist it, you must write the 'export' line into a startup file (~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc, ~/.profile) so it is re-created every time a new shell starts.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The order of directories in PATH does not matter as long as the program is listed.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Order is decisive: the shell runs the first matching executable it finds scanning PATH left to right, so an earlier directory shadows a program of the same name later on. This is precisely how virtualenvs work by prepending their bin, and why 'which python3' can point somewhere you did not expect - fix it by checking the order, not just presence.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Externalizing config in the environment lets one immutable build artifact (a Docker image, a package) deploy to many machines and environments with different values injected per deploy, so you scale by parameterization rather than rebuilding; orchestrators (Kubernetes env/ConfigMaps, ECS task definitions) supply the variables at scale.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Because promoting code between environments changes only the injected variables and not the code path, environment-specific bugs shrink; validate required variables at startup (fail fast with a clear error if DATABASE_URL is missing) so a misconfiguration is caught immediately rather than mid-run.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Keep configuration reproducible and version-controlled (the non-secret parts) so a rebuilt or replaced host comes up with the same environment; never rely on a variable that only exists because someone typed it into a terminal once - define it declaratively in the deploy system.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Track and audit what configuration each service is running with (without logging secret values), and alert when a required variable is missing or a PATH resolves a tool to an unexpected version, since these silently change behavior.
productionConsiderations.security: Treat credentials in the environment as sensitive: never commit .env files, scrub secrets from logs and error reports, restrict who can read a process's environment, prefer a secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault) that injects short-lived credentials, and rotate keys regularly.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Guard against expensive misconfigurations by making environment names explicit (ENV=production) and validating them, so a job never accidentally points a dev run at a production warehouse; preventing leaked credentials also avoids the large cloud bills attackers can generate.
productionConsiderations.performance: Reading environment variables is effectively free, but resolving commands via a long PATH adds tiny per-invocation lookups; keep PATH lean and ordered so the right tool is found first, and rely on the shell's hash cache for repeated calls in hot loops.

codeExamples.title: View, set, export, and unset variables; inspect PATH and resolve commands
codeExamples.overview: Learn the everyday commands to see the environment, create a shell-local vs exported variable, read PATH, and find out exactly which executable a name resolves to.
codeExamples.code:
# 1) List ALL exported environment variables
printenv          # or: env

# 2) Print just one variable (quote it to be safe)
echo "$HOME"
printenv PATH

# 3) Create a SHELL-LOCAL variable (children will NOT see it)
GREETING=hello
echo "$GREETING"        # works in this shell...
bash -c 'echo "[$GREETING]"'   # ...but the child sees it empty: []

# 4) EXPORT it so child processes inherit it
export GREETING
bash -c 'echo "[$GREETING]"'   # now the child sees: [hello]

# 5) Set and export in one step (typical for config)
export LOG_LEVEL=INFO
export AWS_REGION=us-east-1

# 6) See how PATH is built (colon-separated, searched left to right)
echo "$PATH"

# 7) Ask which executable a command resolves to via PATH
which python3
command -v python3        # portable equivalent
type python3              # also shows aliases/builtins

# 8) Remove a variable from the environment
unset GREETING
printenv GREETING || echo "GREETING is now unset"
codeExamples.breakdown: 'printenv' and 'env' dump every exported variable; 'echo "$VAR"' or 'printenv VAR' prints one (quoting protects values with spaces). Assigning 'GREETING=hello' makes a shell-local variable - the child launched by 'bash -c' prints empty brackets because it never received it. After 'export GREETING', the same child now sees 'hello', demonstrating that export is exactly what makes a value cross into a child process. 'export LOG_LEVEL=INFO' is the common set-and-export shorthand. 'echo "$PATH"' shows the colon-separated search list; 'which'/'command -v'/'type python3' report which executable that name resolves to given the current PATH. 'unset GREETING' removes it entirely.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
$ printenv PATH
/home/dataeng/.local/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin
$ echo "$GREETING"
hello
$ bash -c 'echo "[$GREETING]"'
[]
$ export GREETING
$ bash -c 'echo "[$GREETING]"'
[hello]
$ which python3
/usr/local/bin/python3
$ command -v python3
/usr/local/bin/python3
$ unset GREETING
$ printenv GREETING || echo "GREETING is now unset"
GREETING is now unset
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting 'export' is the classic bug: the variable works in your shell but is empty in any program you launch. Not quoting "$VAR" breaks on values with spaces or special characters. 'which' can lie if the shell has cached an old location - run 'hash -r' to clear the cache. Names are case-sensitive and conventionally UPPERCASE for exported config.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use 'command -v' instead of 'which' in scripts - it is a POSIX builtin and more portable. Set a variable for just one command without polluting the shell: 'LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG python3 app.py'. Use 'env | sort | grep -i aws' to quickly find related variables in a crowded environment.

codeExamples.title: Persist a variable and add a directory to PATH in ~/.bashrc, then source it
codeExamples.overview: Make an environment variable and a PATH addition survive new terminals by writing export lines into your shell startup file, and apply them without reopening the terminal.
codeExamples.code:
# 1) Create a personal bin directory for your own scripts/tools
mkdir -p "$HOME/bin"

# 2) Add PATH and a config variable to your startup file.
#    Prepending $HOME/bin means your tools take PRECEDENCE.
cat >> ~/.bashrc <<'EOF'

# --- my data engineering setup ---
export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"
export LOG_LEVEL=INFO
export AWS_REGION=us-east-1
EOF

# 3) Those lines only run for NEW shells. Apply them to THIS
#    shell right now by re-reading (sourcing) the file:
source ~/.bashrc

# 4) Verify: $HOME/bin should now be first in PATH
echo "$PATH"

# 5) Verify the variable is set
printenv LOG_LEVEL

# 6) Prove precedence: drop a script in ~/bin and run it by name
printf '#!/usr/bin/env bash\necho "hello from my bin"\n' > "$HOME/bin/greet"
chmod +x "$HOME/bin/greet"
which greet
greet
codeExamples.breakdown: 'mkdir -p "$HOME/bin"' creates a folder for your own executables. The 'cat >> ~/.bashrc <<EOF ... EOF' block appends export lines to the startup file; because the file runs at shell startup, these lines re-create PATH and the variables for every new session. Prepending '$HOME/bin:$PATH' puts your directory first so your programs win over system ones. 'source ~/.bashrc' re-executes the file in the current shell so you do not have to open a new terminal. 'echo "$PATH"' confirms $HOME/bin is now leftmost, and 'printenv LOG_LEVEL' confirms the variable. Finally, creating an executable 'greet' in ~/bin and running it by name proves the PATH addition works and 'which greet' resolves to it.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
$ source ~/.bashrc
$ echo "$PATH"
/home/dataeng/bin:/home/dataeng/.local/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin
$ printenv LOG_LEVEL
INFO
$ which greet
/home/dataeng/bin/greet
$ greet
hello from my bin
codeExamples.commonIssues: Editing ~/.bashrc does NOT change already-open terminals until you 'source' it or open a new one. On macOS the default shell is Zsh, so use ~/.zshrc instead of ~/.bashrc. Writing 'PATH="$HOME/bin"' without ':$PATH' wipes out the rest of PATH and breaks basic commands - always keep the existing $PATH. Non-login/non-interactive shells (like cron) may not read ~/.bashrc at all.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Prepend for tools that must override system versions; append ('export PATH="$PATH:/opt/tool/bin"') for optional fallbacks. Keep additions idempotent so re-sourcing does not duplicate entries. For system-wide, non-secret variables use /etc/environment or a file in /etc/profile.d/ instead of a per-user file.

codeExamples.title: Configure an ETL script safely with env vars and a .env file (no hardcoded secrets)
codeExamples.overview: Pass a database URL and credentials to a Python ETL job through the environment instead of hardcoding them, then switch to the common .env pattern so you never commit secrets.
codeExamples.code:
# --- Approach A: export directly, then run the job ---

# 1) Provide config via the environment (NOT in the code)
export DATABASE_URL="postgresql://etl:s3cr3t@db.internal:5432/analytics"
export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID="AKIAEXAMPLE"
export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY="wJalrEXAMPLEKEY"
export LOG_LEVEL="INFO"

# 2) The script reads os.environ - no credentials are in the file
cat etl.py
# import os
# db  = os.environ["DATABASE_URL"]            # required: KeyError if missing
# lvl = os.environ.get("LOG_LEVEL", "WARNING") # optional with default
# print(f"Connecting with log level {lvl} to {db.split('@')[-1]}")

python3 etl.py

# --- Approach B: the .env file pattern (local dev) ---

# 3) Put config in a .env file (KEY=value per line)
cat > .env <<'EOF'
DATABASE_URL=postgresql://etl:s3cr3t@db.internal:5432/analytics
AWS_REGION=us-east-1
LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG
EOF

# 4) NEVER commit it - ignore it in git
echo ".env" >> .gitignore

# 5a) Load it into the shell environment (pure bash)
set -a            # auto-export everything defined next
source .env
set +a
python3 etl.py

# 5b) Or let python-dotenv load it inside the script
pip install python-dotenv
# in etl.py:  from dotenv import load_dotenv; load_dotenv()
python3 etl.py
codeExamples.breakdown: Approach A exports DATABASE_URL and AWS credentials into the environment; etl.py reads them with 'os.environ["DATABASE_URL"]' (required - raises KeyError if absent) and 'os.environ.get("LOG_LEVEL", "WARNING")' (optional with a default), so no secret is written in the source. Approach B moves the same values into a .env file of KEY=value lines and adds '.env' to .gitignore so it is never committed. 'set -a; source .env; set +a' auto-exports every variable the file defines into the shell, so python3 inherits them; alternatively python-dotenv's 'load_dotenv()' reads .env from inside the script. Either way the code stays identical while the config (and secrets) live outside it.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
$ python3 etl.py
Connecting with log level INFO to db.internal:5432/analytics
$ set -a; source .env; set +a
$ python3 etl.py
Connecting with log level DEBUG to db.internal:5432/analytics
codeExamples.commonIssues: Committing the .env file is a serious leak - always gitignore it before your first commit. Using os.environ["X"] (bracket) crashes with KeyError if the variable is missing; use os.environ.get("X", default) when it is optional. Values with spaces or special characters in .env may need quoting. python-dotenv does NOT override variables already set in the real environment by default, which is the intended precedence but surprises people.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Validate required variables at startup and exit with a clear message if any are missing, so failures are obvious. Keep separate .env.dev / .env.prod files and load the right one per environment. In production prefer a secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault) or CI/CD secret injection over a .env file on disk, and never log the secret values themselves.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A data team needs one ETL codebase to run in three environments - a developer's laptop, a staging server, and production - each pointing at a different database and using different credentials, without ever hardcoding a secret or maintaining three copies of the code. It must also run correctly under a scheduler where the interactive shell setup does not apply.
endToEndExample.inputData: A single Python ETL script (etl.py) that reads DATABASE_URL, AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, AWS_REGION, and LOG_LEVEL from os.environ, plus per-environment configuration supplied as environment variables (a gitignored .env file locally, injected secrets in staging/prod).
endToEndExample.architecture: Configuration is stored entirely in the environment (Twelve-Factor style): locally a gitignored .env file is loaded (python-dotenv or 'set -a; source .env; set +a'); on servers the variables are injected by the deploy system / secrets manager. A project virtualenv is activated so its bin is prepended to PATH, guaranteeing the tested Python and dependencies run. Startup validation fails fast if a required variable is missing, and secrets are never written to code or logs.
processingSteps: 1. Locally, the developer creates a .env with the dev DATABASE_URL and dev credentials, adds '.env' to .gitignore, and activates the project's virtualenv so 'which python3' resolves to the venv's interpreter (its bin was prepended to PATH).

2. They load the config with 'set -a; source .env; set +a' (or python-dotenv inside the script) and run 'python3 etl.py'; the shell forks/execs Python and the kernel copies the exported variables into the process.

3. etl.py reads os.environ['DATABASE_URL'] (required) and os.environ.get('LOG_LEVEL','WARNING') (optional), validating at startup and exiting with a clear message if any required variable is absent, so misconfiguration fails immediately.

4. For staging, the same code is deployed unchanged; the deploy system injects the staging DATABASE_URL and staging credentials as environment variables (no .env on disk), and PATH is set so the packaged interpreter runs.

5. For production, a secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager or Vault) supplies short-lived credentials as environment variables at container start, and ENV=production is validated so a prod run can never accidentally target the dev warehouse.

6. Under the scheduler, because non-interactive shells may skip ~/.bashrc, the job explicitly sources its environment (or the scheduler sets the variables directly), avoiding the 'works in my terminal but not in cron' trap.
endToEndExample.output: The identical ETL code runs in all three environments, each connected to the correct database with the correct credentials, with no secret present in the source repository and behavior (log level, region, target) controlled entirely by injected environment variables.
endToEndExample.monitoring: At startup the job logs which non-secret settings it is using (environment name, region, log level, and the database host - never the password) and records the resolved interpreter path; alerts fire if a required variable is missing or if PATH resolves an unexpected tool version.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Required variables are validated up front so a missing DATABASE_URL aborts the run with a clear error rather than a confusing mid-run failure; secrets are scrubbed from logs and tracebacks; and reading optional variables via os.environ.get with sensible defaults prevents crashes on absent, non-critical settings.
endToEndExample.finalResult: One codebase, three environments, zero hardcoded secrets: configuration and credentials flow in through the environment, PATH guarantees the right interpreter, startup validation catches misconfiguration early, and the same artifact promotes cleanly from laptop to staging to production - exactly why 'config in the environment' is a foundational data-engineering practice.

industryUseCases.company: SaaS data platforms following Twelve-Factor config
industryUseCases.problem: Teams needed the same application image to run across dev, staging, and production with different databases and credentials, without rebuilding or risking committed secrets.
industryUseCases.solution: Store all config in environment variables injected per environment (Docker -e, Kubernetes env/ConfigMaps, CI/CD secrets), read via os.environ/process.env, with .env files only for local development and gitignored.
industryUseCases.benefits: One build artifact promotes cleanly across environments, secrets stay out of source control, and environment-specific bugs drop because the code path never changes between deploys.

industryUseCases.company: Cloud data engineering teams using AWS
industryUseCases.problem: Pipelines needed AWS credentials and region settings to talk to S3, Redshift, and other services without hardcoding keys that could leak through the repository.
industryUseCases.solution: Provide AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, and AWS_REGION through the environment - locally via a gitignored .env, in production via IAM roles or a secrets manager that injects short-lived credentials at run time.
industryUseCases.benefits: No long-lived keys in code, credentials rotate without code changes, and a single leaked commit can no longer expose the account, dramatically reducing security and cost risk.

industryUseCases.company: Python-centric analytics teams using virtualenvs and dbt
industryUseCases.problem: Different projects required different Python and tool versions, and running the wrong interpreter caused dependency conflicts and 'works on my machine' failures.
industryUseCases.solution: Use virtual environments that prepend their bin directory to PATH on activation so 'python', 'pip', and 'dbt' resolve to the project's exact versions, and set PYTHONPATH/DBT_PROFILES_DIR through the environment.
industryUseCases.benefits: Each project reliably runs its tested toolchain, PATH ordering guarantees the right binaries, and onboarding is faster because activation reproduces the correct environment automatically.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Because configuration lives in the environment, a single immutable artifact deploys to any number of hosts and environments with values injected per deploy; orchestrators (Kubernetes env/ConfigMaps, ECS task definitions, systemd EnvironmentFile) supply variables at fleet scale, so scaling is parameterization rather than code duplication.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Define every variable declaratively in the deploy system and version-control the non-secret parts, so a replaced or rebuilt host comes up with an identical environment; never depend on a value that only exists because it was typed into a terminal, since that is lost on restart.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Inject configuration and secrets at container/process start from a highly-available source (a secrets manager or config service with replicas), so new instances brought up during failover receive the correct environment automatically rather than waiting on a human.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Keep non-secret config in version control and secrets in a managed store with backups and rotation, so a rebuilt environment can be reconstituted quickly; document exactly which variables each service requires so recovery is deterministic.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Reading environment variables is negligible, but a long or misordered PATH adds per-invocation lookups; keep PATH lean, order it so the most-used tools are found first, and rely on the shell's hash cache for repeated command resolution in tight loops.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Prevent expensive misconfigurations by validating environment names (ENV=production) so jobs never target the wrong warehouse, and by keeping credentials out of code to avoid leaked-key incidents that let attackers run up large cloud bills; audit for unused or duplicated variables that cause confusing, costly reruns.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Treat environment-borne secrets carefully: gitignore .env files, scrub secrets from logs and tracebacks, restrict who can read a process's environment (/proc/<pid>/environ), prefer short-lived credentials from a secrets manager, rotate keys regularly, and never bake secrets into images or commit them.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Log the non-secret configuration a service starts with (environment, region, log level, resolved interpreter path) but never the secret values; alert on missing required variables, unexpected PATH resolution (wrong tool version), and drift between intended and actual environment.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Validate required variables and their formats at startup (a well-formed DATABASE_URL, a valid region, a known ENV) and fail fast with a clear message, so a malformed or missing setting is caught before it produces wrong or partial data downstream.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Emit a startup log recording which environment and settings are active (secrets redacted) for auditability, alert when a required variable is absent or a credential fails to load, and record configuration changes so a behavior change can be traced back to an environment change.

recommendedPractices: **Store config in the environment, not code:** keep connection strings, credentials, region, and flags in environment variables so one codebase runs everywhere unchanged.
**Never commit secrets:** put credentials in gitignored .env files locally and in a secrets manager or CI/CD store in production; scrub them from logs.
**Validate required variables at startup:** fail fast with a clear message if DATABASE_URL or a key is missing, rather than crashing confusingly mid-run.
**Keep PATH additions safe and ordered:** always preserve the existing $PATH (':$PATH'), prepend to override, append for fallbacks, and check with 'which'.
**Persist in the right startup file:** use ~/.zshrc (Zsh/macOS) or ~/.bashrc (interactive Bash), and remember non-interactive shells (cron) may need the environment set explicitly.
engineeringStandards: Read config with os.environ.get(name, default) for optional values and os.environ[name] (with startup validation) for required ones, never hardcoding secrets.
Export variables consumed by child processes; use per-command 'VAR=value cmd' for one-off overrides instead of polluting the shell.
Never overwrite PATH wholesale - always extend it relative to the existing $PATH to avoid breaking basic commands.
designRecommendations: Follow Twelve-Factor: anything that varies between deploys belongs in the environment, while stable, non-secret defaults can live in a config file.
Separate how config is provided (shell export, .env, secrets manager) from how the code reads it (os.environ), so the same code runs under any injection method.
Use a virtualenv (which prepends to PATH) per project so the correct interpreter and dependencies are guaranteed without touching system PATH.
namingConventions: Use UPPERCASE_WITH_UNDERSCORES for environment variables (DATABASE_URL, AWS_REGION) to distinguish them from shell-local temporaries.
Follow ecosystem-standard names where they exist (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, PYTHONPATH) so tools pick them up automatically.
Prefix project-specific variables consistently (e.g. MYAPP_DB_URL, MYAPP_ENV) to avoid collisions in the shared, global environment namespace.
documentationStandards: Provide a committed .env.example listing every required variable with placeholder (non-secret) values so new engineers know what to set.
Document which variables are required vs optional, their expected format, and their default for each environment.
Record which startup file and injection mechanism each environment uses, and note any PATH requirements (e.g. the project virtualenv must be active).
testingStrategies: Test that the app fails fast with a clear error when a required variable is missing, and uses documented defaults when an optional one is absent.
Test that the same code behaves differently only via injected variables (e.g. LOG_LEVEL, ENV) with no code changes between environments.
Verify PATH-dependent behavior: assert 'which python3' resolves to the intended interpreter after activating the project environment.

commonMistakes.mistake: Setting a variable without 'export' and then wondering why the program reads it as empty/None.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: The variable works fine when you echo it in the shell, so it looks set - but a plain assignment is shell-local and is never copied into child processes.
commonMistakes.impact: The launched script (python, subshell) sees the variable as missing, causing KeyError, None, or a fallback to a wrong default - often mistaken for a code bug.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use 'export NAME=value' (or 'export NAME' after assigning) so the variable is placed in the environment that fork/exec hands to children, then verify with 'printenv NAME' or from inside the program.

commonMistakes.mistake: Overwriting PATH instead of extending it (writing PATH="$HOME/bin" without ':$PATH').
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Copying a snippet or trying to 'set' PATH like any other variable, not realizing PATH already contains the directories that make basic commands work.
commonMistakes.impact: Commands like ls, git, and even python suddenly fail with 'command not found' because their directories were dropped from the search list, breaking the shell session.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Always keep the existing value: 'export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"' to prepend or 'export PATH="$PATH:/opt/tool/bin"' to append; if you clobbered it, open a new shell to recover the default.

commonMistakes.mistake: Committing a .env file (or hardcoding secrets) to the repository.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: The .env file is created for local convenience and it is easy to forget to gitignore it before the first commit, or credentials get pasted directly into code 'just to test'.
commonMistakes.impact: Secrets leak the moment the repo is pushed, forked, or made public; leaked cloud keys can be exploited within minutes, exposing data and generating large bills.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Add '.env' to .gitignore before your first commit, keep secrets out of code entirely, provide a non-secret .env.example, and use a secrets manager or CI/CD secret store in production.

comparisonSection.explanation: A shell-local variable exists only in the current shell and is usable in that shell, but when you launch a program the child does not receive it because it was never added to the environment block. An exported variable is marked to be copied into every child process via fork/exec, so your Python script or subshell can read it. If a program you run needs the value, it must be exported; if it is only for shell logic, keep it local. Inheritance is one-way: children get a copy and cannot change the parent's environment.

Both add a directory, but position determines precedence because the shell runs the first match scanning left to right. Prepending makes your directory win, so your tool (or a virtualenv's python) shadows any system version of the same name - use this when you must override. Appending makes the directory a fallback, searched only if nothing earlier matches - use this for optional tools you do not want to override system defaults. Both preserve the existing $PATH, which is essential so basic commands keep working.

comparisonSection.optionB: Secrets manager / injected env in production
comparisonSection.explanation: A gitignored .env file is convenient for local development: KEY=value lines loaded into the environment so the code reads os.environ unchanged. It is not secure enough for production, where secrets should come from a managed store (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault) or the deploy system that injects short-lived credentials at run time and supports rotation and auditing. The code stays identical either way - only the injection mechanism differs - which is exactly the benefit of putting config in the environment.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is an environment variable, and how do you view and set one?
beginnerQuestions.answer: An environment variable is a named key=value pair stored in a process's environment that programs read to configure themselves without hardcoding values. You view all of them with 'printenv' or 'env', print one with 'echo "$VAR"' or 'printenv VAR', set a shell-local one with 'NAME=value', and set an exported one that child programs can see with 'export NAME=value'. You remove one with 'unset NAME'.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: The interviewer wants the basic definition plus the everyday commands. Mentioning that programs read them (os.environ) and the view/set/unset trio shows practical familiarity.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is PATH and how does the shell use it?
beginnerQuestions.answer: PATH is a special environment variable holding a colon-separated list of directories. When you type a command name like 'python3', the shell searches those directories left to right and runs the first matching executable it finds, then stops. That is why you can run programs by name without their full path, and why the ordering of directories determines which version runs. You can see it with 'echo "$PATH"' and find what a name resolves to with 'which' or 'command -v'.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Stress the ordered, left-to-right search and 'first match wins'. Naming 'which'/'command -v' and the colon separator demonstrates hands-on understanding.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is the difference between a shell-local variable and an exported one, and why does it matter?
intermediateQuestions.answer: A plain assignment (NAME=value) creates a shell-local variable visible only in the current shell. 'export NAME=value' additionally places it in the environment block that the kernel copies into child processes when the shell forks and execs them. It matters because a program you launch (like a Python script) only inherits exported variables - a non-exported variable will appear missing to that program even though the shell can see it. Inheritance is one-way: children get a copy and cannot modify the parent's environment.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: The key insight is export = inheritance by children, and the one-way copy semantics. Tying it to 'my script reads it as None' makes it concrete.

intermediateQuestions.question: You added a variable in ~/.bashrc but your currently-open terminal does not see it. Why, and how do you fix it?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Startup files like ~/.bashrc are read only when a shell starts, so an already-open shell has not executed the new line. Fix it by re-reading the file in the current shell with 'source ~/.bashrc' (or open a new terminal). Also note the file must be the right one for your shell - ~/.zshrc for Zsh (the macOS default), ~/.bashrc for interactive Bash - and that non-interactive shells (like cron) may not read it at all, which is a common 'works in my terminal but not in cron' cause.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Interviewers want you to know startup files run at launch, the 'source' fix, and the shell-file nuances (Zsh vs Bash, interactive vs non-interactive).

advancedQuestions.question: How do you configure a data pipeline across dev, staging, and production without hardcoding secrets, and why is that the right design?
advancedQuestions.answer: Store all config in environment variables (Twelve-Factor 'config in the environment'): the code reads os.environ for DATABASE_URL, credentials, region, and flags, and the values are injected differently per environment - a gitignored .env file locally (loaded via python-dotenv or 'set -a; source .env; set +a'), and a secrets manager or CI/CD secret injection in staging/production, ideally with short-lived, rotatable credentials. Validate required variables at startup and fail fast. This is correct because the same build artifact promotes across environments with only injected values changing, secrets never enter source control, and environment-specific bugs shrink because the code path is identical everywhere.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Tests production maturity: env-based config, per-environment injection, secrets manager, startup validation, and the Twelve-Factor rationale. Bonus for mentioning gitignore and rotation.

advancedQuestions.question: Explain how PATH ordering causes the 'wrong python' problem and how a virtualenv fixes it.
advancedQuestions.answer: Because the shell runs the first matching executable found scanning PATH left to right, a directory earlier in PATH shadows a program of the same name later. If a system Python appears before the one you intend, 'python3' resolves to the wrong interpreter, causing dependency mismatches. A virtual environment fixes this by prepending its own bin directory to PATH when activated, so 'python' and 'pip' resolve to the venv's copies first. To diagnose, run 'echo "$PATH"' and read it left to right, and 'which python3' to see the resolved path; if the shell cached an old location, 'hash -r' clears it.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Checks understanding of ordering/precedence, the venv-prepends-PATH mechanism, and practical debugging with which/echo $PATH/hash -r.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: A colleague reports that their ETL script works when they run it manually in their terminal but fails with a 'DATABASE_URL not set' error when the same script runs from cron. How do you diagnose and fix it?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: The symptom - works interactively, fails under cron - points at environment differences, not code. Cron runs a minimal, non-interactive, non-login shell that typically does NOT read ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc, so any export they added there is absent. First confirm where DATABASE_URL is defined (likely ~/.bashrc). Confirm cron's environment is bare by having the cron job print its environment. Then make the variable available to cron explicitly rather than relying on interactive startup files. Also verify PATH in cron is complete, since cron's default PATH is minimal and may not find python3.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Recognize that cron uses a minimal non-interactive shell that does not source ~/.bashrc/~/.zshrc, so the exported DATABASE_URL is missing. Fix by providing the environment to the job directly: set the variables in the crontab itself, or have the job source a dedicated env file (or a gitignored .env via 'set -a; source /path/.env; set +a'), or wrap the command in a script that exports what it needs. Also set a full PATH in the crontab (or use absolute paths / the venv's python) because cron's default PATH is minimal. Verify by temporarily having the cron job run 'printenv > /tmp/cronenv' to see exactly what it has.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design how a data team should manage configuration and secrets for a pipeline that must run identically across developer laptops, staging, and production, with different databases and credentials in each.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Adopt 'config in the environment': the code reads all settings from os.environ and hardcodes nothing. Locally, developers use a gitignored .env (with a committed .env.example documenting required keys) loaded via python-dotenv. In staging/production, the deploy system injects variables, with secrets coming from a managed store (AWS Secrets Manager or Vault) as short-lived, rotatable credentials. Use a per-project virtualenv (prepending its bin to PATH) so the tested interpreter runs. Validate required variables at startup and fail fast, and log non-secret settings for observability.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: .env files are simple and need no infrastructure but are unsafe for production secrets and easy to leak if not gitignored; a secrets manager adds setup and dependency but provides rotation, auditing, and short-lived credentials. Environment variables are universal and keep code identical across deploys, but are stringly-typed and unvalidated, so startup validation is needed. Relying on interactive startup files is convenient but breaks under cron/non-interactive shells, so schedulers must be given the environment explicitly.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Move from per-developer .env files to declarative, injected configuration managed by the orchestrator (Kubernetes env/ConfigMaps for non-secrets, a secrets manager for secrets) so one immutable image deploys to many hosts and environments by parameterization. Centralize non-secret config in version control, rotate secrets automatically, validate and log configuration at startup fleet-wide, and standardize variable names so tools and services pick them up consistently.

followUpQuestions: What exactly does 'export' change internally, and why can't a child process modify its parent's environment?
Which startup files does your shell read, and how do login vs non-login and interactive vs non-interactive shells differ?
How is PYTHONPATH different from PATH, and when would you set it?
Why are environment variables convenient but not a strong secrets store, and what should you use instead in production?
How does activating a Python virtualenv change PATH, and how would you verify it with 'which'?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: Environment variables are inherited NAME=value config held per-process (exported ones pass to children); PATH is the colon-separated, left-to-right list of directories the shell searches to find the program you type - persist both by writing 'export' lines into your shell startup file.
keyConcepts: A plain NAME=value is shell-local; 'export NAME=value' makes it inheritable by child processes - inheritance is one-way (parent to child).
PATH is an ordered, colon-separated list; the shell runs the first matching executable scanning left to right, so order sets precedence.
Variables are per-process and vanish when the shell closes; persist them with export lines in ~/.bashrc / ~/.zshrc / ~/.profile.
Editing a startup file has no effect on open shells until you 'source' it or open a new terminal; cron/non-interactive shells may skip it.
Keep secrets out of code: read os.environ, use a gitignored .env locally, and a secrets manager or injected env in production.
commands: printenv                # list all exported variables (or: env)
echo "$PATH"             # print PATH; use printenv VAR for one var
export DATABASE_URL=... # set + export so child programs inherit it
which python3           # show which executable a name resolves to (or: command -v)
export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"   # prepend a dir (takes precedence); keep :$PATH
source ~/.bashrc        # re-read startup file to apply changes now
interviewPoints: export is what makes a variable cross into a child process; without it, programs read it as missing.
PATH is searched left to right, first match wins - this is the 'wrong python' cause and how virtualenvs override.
Variables are per-process and per-session; persist via startup files, which run only at shell startup.
Never commit secrets: gitignore .env, read os.environ, use a secrets manager in production.
cron/non-interactive shells do not read ~/.bashrc, so give them the environment (and PATH) explicitly.
quickNotes: Always quote "$VAR" and keep ':$PATH' when extending PATH so you don't clobber it.
os.environ["X"] raises KeyError if missing; use os.environ.get("X", default) for optional.
'VAR=value command' sets a variable for one command only, without touching the shell.
macOS default shell is Zsh - edit ~/.zshrc, not ~/.bashrc.
python-dotenv does not override real environment variables by default (intended precedence).

keyTakeaways: An environment variable is a per-process NAME=value pair programs read (via os.environ) to configure themselves; a plain assignment is shell-local, and only 'export'ed variables are copied into the child processes you launch - inheritance flows one way, parent to child.

PATH is a colon-separated, ordered list of directories the shell searches left to right, running the first matching executable it finds; ordering therefore sets precedence, which is exactly how virtualenvs override the system Python and why 'which python3' can surprise you.

Environment variables and PATH changes are session-bound and disappear when the shell closes; make them permanent by writing 'export' lines into the correct startup file (~/.zshrc on macOS/Zsh, ~/.bashrc for interactive Bash), remembering that open shells and cron may not see them until sourced or set explicitly.

Keep configuration and especially secrets out of code: read them from the environment, use a gitignored .env file for local development (loaded via python-dotenv or 'set -a; source .env; set +a'), and inject them from a secrets manager or CI/CD in production so one codebase runs across dev, staging, and prod.

Debug env/PATH issues with printenv, echo "$VAR", and which/command -v; always extend PATH with ':$PATH' rather than overwriting it, validate required variables at startup so failures are obvious, and never commit credentials - these habits prevent the most common and most costly configuration mistakes.
